UNIONTOWN, Pa, May 90
The Rabbinical Assembly of
America yesterday condemned
the McCarran-Walter Immigra-
ton law, charged the United
States with supplying arms to
the Arabs and urged the Gov
ernment to ratify the United
Nations convention against
genocide.


The assembly describes itself
as conservative branch of the
Jewish religion.


More than 200 rabbis attend
ing the 54th annual convention
of the assembly unanimously
approved a resolution denounc-
ing the new immigration law.
It said:


"By perpetuating the national
origins quota system, by making
distinctions between natives and
naturalized citizens and by es-
tablishing unfair standards for
exclusion and deportation, our
present immigration policy
makes immoral distinctions
among men,"


The assembly also said the
United States is sending arms to
the Arabs and declared "such
arms will neither promote peace
nor win lasting gratitude"


The assembly unanimously
approved a resolution urging the
United States to ratify the
United Nations convention
against genocide. Genocide is
systematic determination of a
racial, political or cultural group.

= CHATHAM, England. Dec. 16.
Hope was abandoned today for
three civilian dockyard workers
missing since a wall of water
hurled the submarine y Talent
from the Royal Navy drydock
here and left her wallowing on
a mudbank in the Medway River.


Navy divers searched the
wreck early this morning but
found no trace of the missing
men.


A naval spokesman said it
was believed they were swept
away when the drydock's flood
gate burst yesterday afternoon,
letting in a flood that wrenched
the sub from her moorings and
backwashed her into the river.


Thirty lone workmen were
later rescued from atop the bulk.
Three were seriously hurt. Fifty
had scrambled up the drydock
steps to safety as the water
roared in.


The Talent was undergoing a
major refit at the big naval base
here, and all the men aboard
her were dockyard workers.

LONDON, Dec. 4.-The British
press has commented with warm
approval upon the latest stand
of President Eisenhower in the
explosive Far East situation.


Previously there had been
fears expressed in the press and
in official British circles that
American policy in the Far East
might bring on general war.


The recently concluded United
States-C Chinese Nationalist mu-
tual security pact raised new
worries here over the already
tense relations between Red
China and Chang Kai-shek on
Formosa.


But President Eisenhower's
news conference after the pact
was announced has brought
support from much Of the
British press. While denounc-
ing Red China's Imprisonment
of 13 Americans on spying
charges, Gen. Eisenhower coun-
seled against demands for an
immediate naval blockade of
Red China.


1.-THE patience of the President
under what appears to be delib-
crate provocation from Peiping
offers a reassuring interpreta-
ton of the mutual defense pact
negotiated with the Nationalist
Chinese government" said the
conservative Daily Telegraph.


The liberal Manchester Guard
ian said the news conference
"again gave earnest proof of the
moderation and restraint which
have become the foundation Of
his (Eisenhower's) foreign pol
icy. The President, after in
decision earlier this year. is now
directing American policy with
flrmness and purpose"

Gen. Eisenhower's homily on the
duties Of his Office amid the bitter
winds of a cold war was made
with deep conviction, and identi-
fies him even more clearly with
the cause of peace"

land safely near Munich.

which the United States govern

accused the Czech pilot of hav-

PERTH, Australia, April L.
Queen Elizabeth II sailed from
Australia today after a 57-day
visit that won resounding cheers
from her Australian subjects.


The royal liner Gothic steamed
from Fremantle harbor, this
western city's port, as thousands
of onlcokers waved and shouted
good-by and other ships sounded
their whistles.


The next stop on the young
monarch's commonwealth tour
is the Cocos Islands, in the In
dian Ocean 800 miles southwest
Of Singapore. She is due there
April 5.


The Queen, standing on the
top deck with her husband, the
Duke of Edinburgh, looked as
happy and refreshed today as on
February 3, when the Gothic
brought her into Sydney. She
had travelled thousands of miles
across the broad nation and car
ried out $50 formal engagements.

DORTMUND, Germany, Dec.
18.-Fourteen Germans were
killed and 81 injured today when
two trains, one a special carry
ing 500 school children home for
Christmas, collided in predawn
darkness near Dortmund's main
railway station.


None of the children were
killed but three were slightly
injured.


Rescuers probed through the
wreckage OF the regular train
by light of torches and search
lights to recover bodies and lead
survivors to safety. Cutting
torches were used to free some
victims.


Several hours after the crash
the holiday special continued its
trip to Dusseldorf. The chill
dren were en- route to their
homes from school on the North
Sea Island of Sylt.


Rail officials said the other
train was jampacked. The spe-
cial rammed into it, ripping open
one Of the cars.

previous flood and landslides,
we're imperiled by the new
downpour. The rain halted late
in the morning but the skies re-
manned leaden and threatening.

year ago this week end two

on a sailing trip to Macao from
Hong Kong fell into Communist
hands and, so far as official in
formation goes. have not been
heard from since.


Richard Applegate of Medford

York, International News Serv-
ice correspondent who was vaca-
tioning here from Korea. were
aboard Mr.. Applegate's yawl
"Kert" when a Red armed junk
pounced on it, apparently just
outside Hong Kong waters. late
on Saturday afternoon, March
81.


A lookout station on British
Lantao Island saw the captives
and craft taken to the Com
munist-held island of Lapsapmei
and later towed to the main
land Also aboard were Mer-
chantman Capt. Ben Krasner OF
Brooklyn, Capt. Krasner's Chi
nese woman friend, and two
Chinese boat boys.



There have been dozens of
unofficial reports about the cap
tives, but the Communists, in the
press and on the radio. never
have sent a word about them.

Washington's snow-emergency plan passed
its first big test with commendable success.
Until the major snow storm early this week
the Traffic Departments carefully planned pro-
gram for keeping improperly prepared auto
mobiles off the streets during such emergencies
remained in the experimental stage. The
skeptics have been given an impressive demon
Stration of the worth-whileneSS of an emer-
gency traffic-control plan with teeth in it.


Repeated appeals for voluntary cooperation
of drivers in avoiding practices that contribute
to traffic Snarls during snow storms had proved
futile in years past. It was not until car own
ers were threatened with arrest for venturing
on main streets without snow tires or chains
that drivers generally paid much attention to
the problem While some motorists with prop
erly equipped cars sensibly left their cars at
home last Monday, many others tried their
special tires or chains and found them very
effective. Apparently most cars not legally
prepared to cope with emergency conditions
were kept out of the restricted area The few
drivers who forgot the ban or who ignored 1t
were dealt with firmly but considerably by
police, who incidentally, worked overtime to
assist motorists and pedestrians on the slippery
streets.


More snow is predicted in the near future.
If motorists will continue to cooperate in max
ing the new regulation work-a matter of self
interest-the city need have no fear of
repetition of the paralyzng traffic jams that
have developed in times past, even during light
snowfalls

For wears, man and boy, have been
following with mounting puzzlement
the perennial hassles on the erection OF
bridges over the Potomac.


have never been able to understand
why no one has stepped forth with the
obvious solution to this apparently
eternal wrangle: Vehicular tunnels.


Vehicular tunnels are the one solution
that should please every one, and the
one solution that will meet future cross
river traffic problems up and down the
Potomac.


Baltimore, after years of pro and
con, finally realized that tunnel was
the only proper solution for an other
wise impossible traffic problem. New
York and Boston and countless other
cities have found tunnels the thing.


Washington also has been expert
menting with the tunnel idea. For what
are our various underpasses but baby"
tunnels?


Tunnels have definite advantages
over bridges. Esthetically, tunnels can
not interfere with the natural beauty
Of landscape. For instance, tunnel
under Roosevelt Island couldn't pos
sibly affect it. But it could possibly add
something to it by improving the land
scaping on either side of the river bank
around the tunnel entrances.


Navigationally, tunnels could not pos
sibly interfere with river navigation.
Meteorologically. bridges are made
serious traffic hazards by snow, ice,
sleet, wind storms. heavy rains. floods,
etc, whereas tunnels actually offer pro-
lection against the weather


Entrances to tunnels can be located
to draw off heavy traffic before it
reaches the river side, thus speeding up
traffic and reducing traffic hazards and
accidents along the river bank


From civil defense point OF view,
in case of bombing, tunnels can become
effective shelter areas


Bridges are something Of an anach-
ronism in the Goth century.


Gino J. Simi.


Editors note: The idea of tunnel
ing has been considered by officials
every time new bridge was proposed.
but has always been abandoned as
too costly. For instance, it would
cost nearly three times as much to
tunnel as it would to erect a span at
the site of the proposed E street
bridge)

A sick and haggard 34-year-old

She told Of being forced to

with Wet Mini jailers when they
released her and her French
Army prisoner-of-war husband

She did not weep. Her tired,
drawn face seemed drained of
all emotion. But her thin blue
veined hands clutched at the

baby she does not expect to see

She first told her story to

presented supporting letters

Americans had no official COM
ment on her story. Unofficially

valent of $247 to help pay her

Pvt. Andre Pagnon of Paris.

Names Americans.

leans included four officers-a
plane commander Stevenson,

plane was a four-engine Amer
ican Navy craft. She believes it

She recalled today the IL hid

Seized by Japanese.

been searching for the Ameri-

the f1iers.


At the end Of World War II.
she said, the Japanese turned

imprisoned because she was both
o-American and pro-French.

frightful as atomic weapons are,
they should not be banned un-

without reducing conventional
arms would deny the allies a
strength in which they excel
and leave the Russians relatively
stronger.

the coming few years would
probably be filled with economic
difficulties which will tempt the
allied nations to dangerously
slacken their defense efforts.

tenance of the defense effort, de-
psite the Vests improved mill
tary positions and despite money
difficulties. will be the big prob
lem of the immediate future.

MEXICO CITY, Oct. 5.-The
Mexican government said yester-
day it had arrested Jaime Rosen-
berg. Guatemala's former police
chief, and issued warrants for
three other Guatemalan exiles
including ousted leftist President
Jacobo Arbenz Guzman.


Other warrants issued at the
request of the Justice Depart
ment were for former Foreign
Minister Guillermo Toriello and
ex-secret police head Rogelio
Cruz Wer. Both served in Ar
benz's Communist-supported re-
gime which toppled last June.


Modify Usual Hospitality.


Mexico's action modified the
policy of hospitality for political
exiles. The step was taken after
the present Guatemalan govern
ment asked that heads of the
former leftist regime be extra
dited to face trial at home for
alleged crimes, including murder
and torture.


When Guatemalan President
Carlos Castillo Armas' regime

mutilated bodies in the capital.
1t claimed the bodies-beaten.
slashed, f1ogged, eyeless and
toothless-were those of men
Arbenz's secret police had tor
tured to death.


Long Fight Possible.


That the arrests were made
did not mean the exiles would
soon be on their way home.
Standard procedure is for the
courts to recommend action in
extradition cases to Mexico's
President, who then makes the
decision. Any decision by Presi-
dent Adolfo Ruiz Confines can
be appealed to the Supreme
Court. This legal procedure
could take from two to four
years.


The Guatemalan government,
in seeking Rosenberg's extradi-
ton, charged him with homi-
eide and embezZlement.


The ex-police chief, permitted
by Justice Department officials
to talk briefly with newsmen.
denied the charges. saying:


"I didn't kill anybody in Guate-

to Mexico in a private plane
after the Arbenz regime toppled.
Arbenz was among those taking
refuge in the Mexican embassy
in Guatemala City who flew here
later in Mexican planes.

All through 1854, mysterious clippings
and scribbled notes have cluttered the top
right-hand drawer of the desk, causing one
to wonder II foreign power has set up its
Intelligence headquarters in ones own
home. But one discovers, at last, the nature
OF these .scribblings and clippings They
are spread now throughout the kitchen,
noted when one wanders into that sanctum
for drink of water or an inspection of the
refrigerator's contents. They are, one sees,
recipes for preparing staples and goodies
for Thanksgiving.


They are, mostly, formulas drawn for
the busy housewife, who In these modern
times must spend much OF her busy day
scanning newspapers and magazines for
tine-saving recipes. They point to quick,
easy ways to prepare the Thanksgiving tur-
key, the dressing, the cranberry sauce, the
pudding. But more, they include items
which never graced the traditional Thanks
giving table sauces to mask the taste Of
the turkey, spices to enhance the cram
berries, goo for the pudding And, finally,
there are hints for decorating the festive
board 50 that suf1cient obstacles win be
placed between turkey and diner.


One emissions a nightmarish table, set
in trice, with quickly prepared food that
allows no time for enticing aromas to per-
meate the house. Such an eventuality
would dampen the holiday spirit, for much
Of the Thanksgiving enjoyment lies In the
predinner anticipation, whetted by odors
from the roasting turkey. One suspects,
however, after bit OF rejection, that the
person charged with preparing the holiday
feast has over-reached herself with all these
clippings and notes, and that the day OF the
feast viii be as III the past, with one more
thing for which to be thankful the tradi-
tional turkey. crNpberry sauce and puddingA

forced to leap into the arms of a
man who helped break the fall.


Five engine companies and

O'Neal of truck company 10,
both colored, donned gas masks
and pushed into the home.


Reach Children.





They reached the children and
passed them through a window
to other f1remen on ladders. The
children were taken to the hos
pital in a rescue squad ambu-
lance.

fire did not reach the victims,
but that they were exposed to
intense heat.

downstairs, the back and middle
rooms being burned out. The
children's father. a District
street sweeper, was at work at

While the Nations leading experts on auto
motive safety are studying their favorite sub
ject they might give a little attention to the
need for built-in safety devices in some cars
Recent news stories have indicated that more
research in this special field of accident preven
ton would be well worth while.


Only few days ago an Alexandrian mar
rowly escaped serious injury or death when the
hood of his automobile suddenly flew up, cauS-
ing him to swerve the car into guard rail. An
eight-inch- thick section of the rail pierced the
front of the car and came to rest against the
drivers seat. Not long ago a child was killed
when his head was caught in automatically
raised automobile window, the mechanism of
which started operating when another child
pushed button.


Some automobiles have been provided with
safety catches which prevent the accidental
release of the hood. Many cars, however, have
only single latch holding the hood down. The
number of accidents resulting from accidentally
sprung hoods may be relatively few, considering
other motoring hazards, but any driver who has
had the frightening experience while driving
on a busy highway will testify that safety
catch for hoods ought to be standard equipment
on all cars. And there ought to be some way of
making automatically controlled windows less
dangerous for car occupants, especially children.
Motorists have enough accident hazards to con-
tend with on the highways without having to
worry about hazards In their own cars that
could have been corrected at the factory. 4

ANNAPOLIS, Jan. 26.-In-
formed sources report that Gov.
McKeldin plans to balance the
States next budget by collect
ing a utility tax twice in one
fiscal year.


The proposal would not only
keep the budget out of the red,
but would avoid the necessity of
a tax increase in an election
year. The Governor already has
announced his opposition to tax
increases.


The levy. which now falls due
in August. applies to gross re-
ceipts in the preceding calendar
year. Public service firms such
as gas. electric and telephone
companies carry the biggest
load. Railroads. safe deposit
and trust companies also con-
tribute.


Would Pay Twice.


Under the plan. the utilities
would pay twice in the 1855 fiscal
year. once next August and
again in June. 1855. The SIS
million anticipated from the tax
would be doubled for the fiscal
year.


Since firms would merely adj
vance second payment by two
and not actually pay in
creased taxes, the Governor and
his aides expected little opposi-
ton to the plan. After the COM
ing fiscal year. the gross receipts
tax would revert back to the
once-a-year plan.


No Tax Cut Seen.


Personal income tax cuts Of Is
percent have been in effect for
the past two years, but the Gov
ernor said similar relief this year
impossible.


With elections coming UP in
the fall. neither the Legislature
nor the Governor would welcome
higher taxes to balance the
budget.


Democrats. however, have been
talking Of chopping the Cover
nor'S money bill again. Cuts of
more than SIS million were

The United States has fired a
final hydrogen explosion in the
1854 test series at the mid-Pa-
cific proving ground which
stirred worldwide controversy.


A joint Atomic energy Com
mission Defense Department an
nouncement said last night the
series had been completed and
"the tests were successful in the
development Of thermonuclear
weapons.


This was much like language
used to mark the, end Of previous
test series and. like the previous
announcements, it did not
specify how many bombs had
been set of. However, three
previous explosions had been
announced-a mighty blast on
March /. another explosion 26
days later and a third on April
6-leaving open to speculation
whether one or more than one
detonation occurred after that
time.


"Thermonuclear" is the scien-
lists term indicating a hydrogen
explosion.


Comedies With Conference.


Announcement of the end of
the series which drew foreign
protests because radioactive
particles showered well outside
the test area, came on the same
day that a f1ve-power conference
opened in London, aimed at
ending the arms race and out
lawing nuclear weapon warfare.


There was some speculation of
a connection between the timing
of yesterdays announcement,
continuing protests abroad and
the London conference. Besides
the usual laconic statement that
a test series had been concluded
successfully. the joint announce
ment by Acc Chairman Lewis
Strauss and Defense Secretary
Wilson also said of the 1854
tests:


'"They were essential to our
national interest and have con-
tributed materially to the Sc
curity of the United States and
the free world.


1.-THE tests being concluded,
within a few days sea and air
traffic may be safely resumed
within the warning area which
was set up for safety purposes
for the time when the tests were
taking place. Official notice to
airmen and mariners will be
published"


This could have been an in
direct reply and assurance by the
Acc and defense chiefs, with
diplomatic guidance, to the COM
plants abroad.


Although the only foreign ma
tionals actually injured by radio
active matter drifting from the
test area have been Japanese
fishermen. some of the sharpest
criticism of the American tests
has come from within Britain.


The fact that the United
States announced yesterday the
1854 series was ended did not
necessarily mean that the pro-
gram had been cut short, al
though this was possible. In
previous Pacific series, using
only atomic" or nuclear fission
explosions instead of the massive
hydrogen blasts, the number of
test explosions usually has been
only half dozen or fewer.


The 1854 thermonuclear test
series produced, lacking any con-
tlicting claims from Russia, the
greatest man-made explosion in
history.

Americans, we prefer obviou;

NANGAL DAM, India, July 8.
Prime Minister Nehru today
opened India's new concrete and
tile-lined Nangal canal system,
longest irrigation network in the
world.


Mr.. Nehru pressed a button
opening the gates of Nangal
Dam. 225 miles north of New
Delhi in the Himalayan foot
hills. Waters of the Sutlej River
eushed into the canals, which
include one channel 240 miles
long.


India is building a sprawling
1927 million hydroelectric and
irrigation project embracing the
Nangal system and nearby
Bhakra Dam without any foreign
financial help. Construction
work on the Bhakra project is
under the supervision of 66-year-
old American Harvey Slocum,
who built the Grand Coulee and
Shasta Dams in the United
States. When finished, the go
foot Bhakra Dam will be the
second highest in the world,
topped only by the 726-foot
Hoover Dam in the United States.

commonwealth.

tant glimpse of the parade
through the English Channel.

cleaning red and white amid

Elizabeth, her husband, the Duke
Of Edinburgh, and their chill
dren, Prince Charles and Prin-
cess Anne. Charles and Anne
had Joined the tour at Tobruk,

Libya, for the final visits to
Malta and Gibraltar.

armada, headed by the battle
ship Vanguard, contacted the
Britannia. which had spent the
night at anchor in st. Austell
harbor on the Cornish Coast.


The Vanguard and the fast
Minelayer Apollo fired a thun-
derous welcoming salute. Then
the rest of the war vessels swung
into positions on either side of
the Britannia for the procession.


From every Southern English
port excursion vessels and yachts
put out for a closer glimpse of
the royal convoy. Overhead jet
aircraft circled and dipped in
salute.

south coast will take all day.

reach the mouth of the River
Thames tomorrow morning. The

workers returned to work today,

area atomic energy plant since

Mediator George Bell.

ized. Union and company Off
cials appeared reluctant to talk

the result of a misunderstanding,

turned over too soon to the Good

operate the plant for the Atomic
Energy Commission. Thus, he

handled by production workers

in the Soviet zone Of Germany

"The Sistine Madonna will be
returned as soon as the Dresden
Art Gallery is reconstructed. We
now have peace again and there
exists no danger any more for
these irretrievable art treasures. .


The Raphael and other Dres-
den Gallery treasures were stored
inside an unused railway tunnel
in East Germany during the war.

Authorities concerned with juvenile delin-
quency have reason to be dismayed by the in
creasing gravity of the problem as revealed in
the annual FBI statistical bulletin, Uniform
Crime Reports. Using new reporting system,
the bulletin provides more comprehensive
and accurate picture Of youthful crime trends
than heretofore has been available. The figures
show an per cent rise in juvenile crime, as
compared with 2 per cent increase in adult
offenSes.


The report for 1858 is the first which offered
basis for comparison with past delinquency
reports. This is because, until 1852, the only
data available for appraising the juvenile crime
rate were f1ngerprints sent to the FBI by police.
But these figures were inaccurate, for the
reason that many Jurisdictions do not finger
print juvenile prisoners. In order to obtain
more complete information on youthful crimi-
nality, the FBI prevailed on police agencies
in 1852 to begin submitting age data in connec-
ton with arrest reports. The 1852 figures.
under the new system, could not be fairly COM
pared with prior totals compiled from finger
print records. It was not until the totals for
1858 had been prepared that any reasonably
accurate estimate Of juvenile crime trends, on
national scale, became available


For purposes of the compilation, the FBI
lists all arrests of persons under Is as juvenile
cases. The report disclosed that last year the
crime rate among these teen-agers rose much
more sharply than that for all other age groups.
Persons under Is accounted for Is per cent of
all the major crimes committed last year.
Those under 81 were responsible for SOC per
cent of Grimes against property" namely, rob-
berry, burglary, larceny, automobile theft, en-
bezzlement, fraud, dealing in stolen property,
forgery and counterfeiting. Delinquents II or
younger were involved in nearly 54 per cent of
all Stolen-car cases last year. 49 per cent of the
burglaries, 40 per cent of the larcenies and 18
per cent of the holdups.


The FBI bulletin does not attempt to place
the blame for these disturbing figures But
FBI Director Hoover, in recent article in the
Syracuse Law Review, said study of notorious
criminal cases indicated that most delinquency
was rooted in unsatisfactory home conditions,
was nurtured by community inadequacies,
especially with respect to churches, schools and
recreational facilities, and was further encour-
aged by misguided "coddling" of youthful
offenders by some parents and law enforcement
officials Washington unfortunately, has not
been free from such shortcomings-as the local
prevalence of juvenile delinquency attests.

officials were cautious in their

Ocean Grove, N. j., where the
Church of the Brethren held its
annual conference last week. still
Eretains much of the charm of a
past era.


A person stepping from nearby
busting Asbury Park into the
grove feels as Though he has
gone from a noisy sideshow into
a quiet church.


The self-contained area, a
popular place for church meet
ings. is probably best known for
its Sunday auto ban. Not only
are autos forbidden to move on
the Sabbath, but they must be
outside the grove from midnight
Saturday to midnight Sunday.


Big Grove Era Recalled.


But even during the week the
area recalls a bygone period.
There is an obvious slowing down
Of tempo among those leiSurely
Strolling beneath the numerous
shade trees or congregating in
the little park before the spa
cious auditorium. Asphalt walks
criSScross the park, and benches
are set beside the walks or fur
ther back on the grass.


Canvas-topped tents line many
Of the side streets. Along Gen.
tennial Park leading to the ocean
are hotels and boarding houses,
their wide porches and comfort
abel-appearing rocking chairs
recalling a gracious past.


The grove goes back nearly a
century, to 1869, when the first
religious service was held there
on July 81. A few months later
the Ocean Grove Campmeeting
Association was formed.


Gates Up in 1873.


Gates setting off the area were
put up at the Main avenue
entrance in 1873. They were
replaced by iron gates in 1890
and by the present stone pillars
in 1916.


The auditorium, seating 10000
persons, was erected in 1894 to
replace one built in 1876. Airy
and comfortable, the building
has numerous electric lights run
ming like lighted beads across
the roof overhead.


Presidents and other famous
personages have spoken at grove
meetings, Theodore Roosevelt,
William Mckinley, Woodrow
Wilson, William Howard Taft
and William Jennings Bryan
have appeared at the auditorium
during the years.


Great singers have also thrilled
crowds there. They included
Nine. Schumann-H eink, John
Mccormack, Galli-Curci, Law
renee Tibbett, Grace Moore and
Giovanni Martinelli.

LONDON, Jan. 4.-Western
Europe's dikes and sea walls,
age-old bastions against the
raging ocean,, stood strong and
firm today after "a hours Of
battering by gale-churned seas.


Anxious watchers. remember
ing when lood waters burst
through the dikes and wrecked
vast areas Of the Low Countries
and Eastern England last Febru-
ary, sighed with relief as they
watched the seas die down to-
day.


In England. police and coast
guards kept an all-night vigil
In low coastal areas, then left
their watch as weathermen re-
ported soon after 10 am. that
the crisis hour of high tide had
passed safely. A collier ran
ashore at Shoreham, Southern
England.


In the Netherlands. where
overnight water levels were the
highest since last winters floods
In which 1,795 persons died, the
situation was reported nearly
back to normal.


Denmark Also Suffers.


But the storm which smashed
the calm Of Europe's winter with
sudden force yesterday still
ragged in many places. Billiards
and heavy snowfalls were re-
ported from Scandinavia down
to Italy.


In Denmark, the little Jutland
town Of Randers was flooded
during the night by the worst
gale in several years. Towns
folk rowed today through wa
ter-logged streets to salvage
their belongings. Rescue squads
in rubber dinghies borrowed
from the army pitched in.


In Odense. salvage workers
toiled with sandbags to patch
up dikes protecting the town
from a nearby canal. which
threatened to burst its banks.


Two ships ran aground of
the North German coast in a
snowstorm.


Swedish Traffic Tangled.
Swedish road. rail and air
transport was snarled after an
80-mile-an-hour blizzard swept
the country. Stockholm airport
was snowbound. roads in North
ern Sweden were completely
blocked by deep snowdrifts, and
some rail services were can
celed. Several coastal vessels
were reported missing.
In Italy, too, heavy snowfalls
particularly in the Alpine re-
gionS-blocked roads and delayed
trains. Weathermen reported
more snow on the way.
Other parts Of Europe were
untouched. London and Brussels
basked peacefully under clear
skies and brilliant sunshine.
From Paris and Oslo came re-
ports Of fair weather and tenn
peratures normal for the time
OF year.

Who remembers the old fashioned
corner grocery store?


Washington in those days was rich
with them. The proprietor was usually,
but not always, a rich old German,
often still talking broken English.


There was bell fixed to the door. so
that when the customer crossed the
threshold, the bell rang ding ding.


The grocer would hurry out from be-
hind the green curtain.


He may have stumbled over the store
cat, or barked his shins on the barrel
of pickles, coal oil, or apples in season.


There was no iron stove in the tradi-
tional New England fashion, for the
National Capital was never New Eng
landish, it was rather Southern in most
of its aspects.


The corner grocery was the place
Johnny was sent scurrying to when the
family ran out of bread, which seemed
rather inevitable in those days.


Mother never had enough bread. The
lady next door may have done a little
polite sneering, when she saw Johnny
run for the store before o'clock, but
it didn't worry mother in the least.

graham with a taste and especially

HANOI, Indo- China, April g.
The weary defenders of Diem
Bien Phu beat off wild new Wet
Mini attacks today. They held
the Communicated rebels at bay
a mile from the heart of the be-
sieged dust bowl fortress.


French counterattackS. backed

A brief French communique

In tidal waves of infantry, brav-

Communicated rebels had pushed
to within a mile of the fortress
center in some places.


The outnumbered French
Union garrison chung desperately

bunkers and barbed wire. But
they were in grave danger. The

Casualties Soar.


Wet Mini casualties scared

10000 killed or wounded since
they swept down on the fortress
in mid-March. The French
claimed 1000 of those were
killed.


The French have not an
nounced their own losses.


I'm Paris, officials said the
defenders of Diem Bien Phu
had suffered heavy" losses,
but light by comparison with

The most serious threat to

western sector of the dust bowl
plain, where the Wet Mimi hold
one position for launching at
tacks. 1t was feared a massive
charge from there and a break
through might carry the attack
erS into the key center area.


Assaults Rise in Tempo.


Heavy and violent Wet Mini
assaults ragged throughout the
night, increasing in tempo in
the early hours before dawn.
But wherever the rampaging
troops tried to break through,
French guns took a heavy toll
and hammered them back. The
French command said it's posi-
ton was substantially the same
as last night.


In two counter-attacks in the
northwest yesterday, the French
drove the Wet Mimi from a cap
tured position. Then the French
Withdrew from the outlying post
because it was so shattered by
artillery fire and bombing it was

The French took heart from

dozen counterattacks kept the
Wet Mimi from charging
through.


Attackers Use Every Weapon.

from the northwest and south
east. First came their heavy
artillery barrages from the sur
rounding hills. Then infantry
men rushed the French barri-
cades, hurting grenades and

through the barbed wire mazes.

finally welded long knives and

hand-to-hand fighting.


Charging en- maSse across the
plain. the rebels afforded easy
targets for the American-sup-

the French Union defenders.
Tanks. artillery and fighter and
bomber attacks also took a heavy
toll.


A French army headquarters
spokesman said yesterday morale
was high within Diem Bien Plus

getting all the ammunition and
other war supplies they need by
parachute drops, and from time
to time reinforcements also have
been parachuted in.

cessive hits off Camilo Pascual
with none out in the ninth in
ning-and while Washington's
bullpen was mysteriously mac
tive-gave the Red Sox three
runs and a 7-6 victory over the
Senators today, dealing them a
second-division finish for the
eighth straight year.


The Senators entered the ninth

visioned a triple tie with Detroit
and Boston going into the final
day of the season, what with
the Indians Ill triumph over
the Tigers showing on the score
board.


'Bucky Harris, the Senator's

had Maury McDermott warming

him to quit throwing while the
Red Sox cannonaded Pascual

fourth-place contention.


Game Ends in Hard Rain.


The game was finished in a
driving rain, under lights, which
made pitching virtually an i'm
possibility on a slick, muddy
mound. 1t could be that Harris
felt no pitcher would be effective
under such conditions.


Sam Mele, who earlier had
slammed a three-run homer to
tie the score at 3-3, started
Boston's ninth-inning rally with
a single to left. Jim Piersall
doubled, and in rapid success
sion. Sammy White, Grady Hat
ton and Billy Console each
singled across a run to give
Boston a one-game lead over
Detroit in the scramble for
fourth.


Big Jim Lemon had provided
the big blow of the game until
that point with a 415-foot, two
run homer in the sixth inning
against Tom Hurd after Roy
Sievers had walked. The blow
into the centerfield bleachers
broke a 3-3 tie and gave the
Senators a lead they didn't re-
linquish until the unhappy ninth.

The Senators battered starter
Willard Nixon for three runs in
the fourth inning after the Red
Sox Highlander retired the first
nine batters in order. Wayne
Terwilliger started the uprising
with walk and Pete Runnels
singled. Mickey Vernon flied out,
but Jim Busby doubled to score
Terwilliger.


Sievers was purposely passed
to jam the bases and Lemon
singled to center, scoring Run
nels and leaving the bases filled.
Ed Fitzgerald also singled, scor-
ing Busby, but Hurd replaced
Nixon and disposed of Jerry
Snyder on a foul to Mele. Hurd
then tossed out Johnny Schmitz.

EAGLE PASS, Tex. July a.
The Rio Grande was back in its
banks today. its receding waters
carrying the secret Of how many
died and leaving mounds Of
foul, diSease-breeding mud.


Hidden in the muck and in
the draining waters was the
answer to whether the best
available figures-62 dead. 80 to
400 missing-fall short Of the
truth.


President Eisenhower declared
the stricken borderland eligible
for disaster loans. Gov. Allan
Shivers' own State disaster task
force flew to the border to work
with the Federal people. The
Red Cross, the Salvation Army
and individuals had little rest.


Clothing, food, medicine,
money-they were on the way
and the need was great.


Piedras Negras Hard Hit.


The need was greatest across
the river in Piedras Negras.
whose announced toll is 80 dead
and 80 missing. One Mexican
army major said the dead there
may number more than 400. He
said it probably never will be
known how many bodies floated
downstream or how many were
recovered and buried by the
bereaved digging with bare
hands into mud heaps which
once were homes.


Twenty-Five bodies had been
recovered by nightfall last night.


Nuevo Laredo, sister Mexican
city Of Laredo, Tex, counted its
first dead-the bodies of five
members Of q family identified
only as Gomez. They were re-
covered yesterday.


Pride Retards u. s. Aid.


Mexican pride prevented de-
livery Of aid which the United
States was anxious to send across
the river. Apparently protocol
demands q formal request from
the Mexicans. The request was
not forthcoming, although every
one here knew food, medicine,
water and technical help were
needed in Piedras Negras.


Twenty thousand persons who
left their homes in the Mexican
cities were returning to the
cleanup job.


For 200 miles there is not a
bridge intact across the Rio
Grande. Rich tourist traffic into
Mexico and export freight will
be affected for weeks.

SOFADHES. Greece. May l.
A warning tremor-coming min
utes before a catastrophe"
earthquake hit Central Greece
was credited today with saving
hundreds of lives.


The quake shook nearly 1000
square miles of Thessaly yester-
day. killing an estimated 90 per-
sons and causing millions of dol
lars in property damage. About
1870 persons were reported in
iured.


The preliminary tremor ratified
dishes and rang bells in So
fadhes and Farsala, the two
hardest hit towns. That shudder
was all the town-folk needed.


I'VE rushed into the streets
and fields and saw our houses
and buildings gradually shake
to pieces one survivor said.


Heavy Damage Reported.


An elderly woman in Sofadhes
said "the first shock saved us.
1t was a warning by God and we
rushed out of our houses. A few
minutes later, the heavy one
struck and the earth continued
shaking for about two minutes.
But it seemed like two hours.
saw my own house gradually
crumple before my eyes"


Karditsa, Trikala and Volos all
reported heavy damage. The viii
lagos of Lechonia, Palamas,
Leontari. Vrisse and Agia Marina
were left with few buildings
which did not have cracked
walls and broken roofs.


Relief supplies were being
rushed to the area and bread
stations already were operating
in several stricken towns.


Communications were gradu-
ally being restored throughout
the area which extended from
Greece's east coast inland to in
accessible mountain terrain.


Thousands without Shelter.


Houses and buildings collapsed
like cards leaving tens of thou
sands of persons without shelter.
This town of 5000 about 40 miles
southwest of Larisa was left vir-
tually without a habitable build
ing. It's main street was choked
with debris.


Buildings reinforced with steel
were twisted into grotesque
shapes. The entire roof and two
walls of a new granite church
collapsed.


Virtually everyone in Thesaly
slept out in the open last night
even in towns where the shocks
were light. Most inhabitants
fearful that recurring quakes
might topple already weakened
houseS-planned to remain out
doors until the danger is over.


Athens Observatory recorded
five more shocks in the quake
stricken area today.

NEW YORK. Sept. 25.-Fed-

yesterday denied defense motions
to dismiss the indictment against
13 Puerto Rican Nationalists
charged with seditious conspir-
acy to overthrow the United
States Government.


Defense attorneys argued there
was not sufficient evidence to
connect the defendants with the
crime. One attorney asked for a
mistrial on the grounds that an
FBI informant who appeared as
Government witness had taken
part in defense conferences.

13 Puerto Ricans on trial are
guilty of "conspiring to over
throw, put down and destroy by
force the Government of the
United States" If convicted,
they face six years in prison and
a $1,000 fine.


Among the defendants are four
Puerto Ricans who last March l
opened fire from the spectators
gallery in the House of Repre-
sentatives, wounding five Con-
gressmen. The four were con-
.victed for the shooting earlier in
Washington and are now being
tried on the conspiracy charges.


The trial resumes Monday.

The Government reported
today that living costs declined
in October for the third straight
month.


The drop of two-tenths of l
per cent from September will
mean a penny hour pay cut
for 10000 workers in the
auto, aircraft and farm ma
chinery industries whose union
contracts call for pay rates
changes geared to the living
cost index.


Food prices, averaging one
half Of per cent lower. were
the main factor in the overall
living cost drop between Sep
tember and October.


The index kept by the Labor
Departments Bureau Of Labor
Statistics eased to HAS per cent
of the 1919 average-the
lowest point this year and the
lowest since June, 1853.


Near I Per Cent.


The living cost level this Oc-
tober is eight-tenths of / per
cent below the record established
in October of last year.


Mrs. Aryness Joy Wickens.
acting labor statistics commits
sioner, indicated at a news con-
ference that current retail prices,
particularly for food. are even
lower in November. She limited
this would mean a further de-
cline in the index when Novem-
Der figures become available
next month.


Mrs. Wickens said nearly all
the makings of the traditional
Thanksgiving dinner are con-
siderably lower this year than
at last Thanksgiving.


Dinner Costs Down.


"We havn't figured how much,
but it is quite clear from every
thing we have that the Thanks
giving dinner costs this year will
be less than last year." she said.


She said turkey prices are
about 4 to 10 cents a pound
cheaper this year, with the big
gest savings for the larger birds.
She said prices for eggs, milk,
sweet potatoes, butter, celery are
all lower this Thanksgiving, but
bread, coffee, lettuce and cram
berries are slightly higher.


The most important food price
cuts between September and Oc-
tober were in pork and poultry.
Fresh fruits were lower, but
fresh vegetables were higher.


A bumper crop brought lower
prices for apples. except in New
England, where the fall hurri-
canes damaged apple crops.

The French bombed, strafed

ging in only 200 yards from the
main barbed-wire barricades of
the fortress.

northwest Indo-C Chinese strong
hold in the heart of the noun
famous Thai country which bor-
ders on Red China.


No Frontal Attack.


There were no screaming
frontal assaults by the enemy,
however, as marked the first

open battle in the Seven-year
war against the forces of Mos
cow-trained Ho Chi Mini.


But Wet Mimi artillery con-
tinued to pour into the "a

and the enemy carried out
elaborate digging-in operations
near the fortified area. This in
dicated they intended to try to
crush the French at Diem Bien

tary victory of the war.

relentleSsly shelled ambulance

ings making it more and more
difficult to evacuate the wounded
from the area. There was no
indication, however, how the
transport, helicopter and para
chute airlift which has supplied
the encircled fortress was far
ing.

The Wet Mini turned deaf
ears on broadcast appeals from
the French for a brief cease
fire to permit the removal of
sick and wounded by plane.
After the first series of wild, all
most suicidal Wet Mini attacks

the French agreed to stop shoot

Assembly, over Soviet-bloc OPP
position, came out last night for
wider sharing Of the burdens Of
any future U. N. military action
to stop aggression.


The 60-nation Assembly also
extended the life of it's 4-year-
old, l4-member Collective Meas
ures Committee, which had rec
commended this principle.


The Assembly also decided,
without dissent, to debate Soviet
charges of United States aggres-
sion and Nationalist China piracy
off the Red China mainland.


One complaint accuses the
United States of aggression
against the Peiping government
through its protection of Nation
alist-held Formosa.

list China, aided by the United
States, with piracy in the seizure
of merchant vessels trading with
Red China.


The Collective Measures Com
mittee said that in any u. N.
fight on aggression, countries
able to contribute both military
forces and equipment and sup
plies should share the latter with
countries able to contribute mill
tary forces only.


The Assembly noted with ap-
prevail this and other principles
contained in the committees
latest report, in passing a reso-
luton recommended by its Politi-
cal Committee. The vote was 48
in favor and 5 against tthe
Soviet Union, the Ukraine, White
Russia, Czechoslovakia and Po-
land. India and Indonesia abb
stained.


Sponsors of the resolution
were Australia, Belgium, Brazil,
Britain, Canada. Egypt, France.
Mexico, the Philippines, Turkey.
the United States and Venezuela.

BALBOA, Canal Zone, Sept.
30.-A United States airlift of
relief supplies for f1ood-ravaged
Northwest Honduras swung into
full operation today.


Transports from Albrook Air
Base here were loaded with
emergency rations, medicine,
water-purifying equipment and
dismantled helicopters. The
helicopters were for reassembly
in Honduras and use on relief
and rescue missions to isolated
areas.


One report said between 1000
and 1000 flood victims were ma
rooned on rooftops and in trees.


Rains Since Hurricane.


The floods are result of heavy
rains which have lashed Hon
duras without letup since Hur-
ricane Gilda struck Monday.
The rampaging waters con-
tinued today to wash through
vast banana tracts. All planta-
tions between Progreso and Ur-
raco and from Buffalo to Tibom-
DO were said to be totally under
water. La Lima, Chameleon
and San Pedro Sula were hard
hit.


A number of villages have
been flooded and isolated, with
roads and railway tracks washed
out and telegraph service cut off
Many persons fed to high
ground. however, and the loss
OF life was described as light.


Landslide Buries Refugees.


Radio reports heard in Ell Sal
vador said several persons were
drowned in La Lima. Others
repeatedly were killed there
when a landslide buried a truck
load of fleeing refugees.


1t. Gen. William K. Harrison,
United States Caribbean COM
mander. said after a flight over
Honduras yesterday that the
flood was not the major disaster
feared at first. He said the
Honduran government had the
situation under control but out
side help still was needed.


Honduran President Juan
Manuel Galvez personally di-
rected rescue operations.

Excelsior from Chiapas' capital.

jalon in the tropical, coffee grow

The first dispatch said the
tremor leveled the towns of va
jalon, Petalcingo. Chilon and
lila. Latest word was that the
ground was still shaking.


Rescue Teams.


Rescue teams with medicines,
food and temporary shelter was
dispatched over primitive roads
to the disaster zone.


Federal and State authorities
were dealing with the situation
as though faced with a major
disaster. Military and civil es-

modified to organize rescue
crews. Planes were flown into

aid supplies. An offer of assist

malan government.

seismographs in New York, Bos-
ton, Cleveland, Pasadena and
other distant points.

assault-suddenly stopped Sun
day-was resumed with new fury
before dawn today as violent
rain storm lashed the battered
fortress.


Rains Slow Down Tanks,


The moment appeared right
for the rebels to make another
attempt to smash the bastion.
The drenching rains slowed
down tanks operating inside the
CONSTRUCTED fortress defenses and
forced French war planes to
cease their strikes against the
attackers.


Before the attack on the west
was launched, the French esti-
mated that the Wet Mimi would
have to cover some 600 yards be-
fore they could stab into the
heart Of the fortress. But they
had to cover only about 100 feet
to reach the first French barbed
wire barricades and to engage
the defenders in hand to hand
combat.


The French high command
communique this morning indi-
Gated the renewed rebel push did
not have the same scope OF
Saturdays assault.


The last attack had come from
all sides of the hemmed- fort
resS, now reduced to less than
a mile across. Before the rebels
halted their wild charges Sun
day, they overran French
strong points guarding the west
ern. eastern and northeastern
approaches to the command
headquarters of Brig. Gen.
Christian de CaStries.


This mornings communique
made no mention of any attack
other than from, the west, one
OF the areas in which the rebels
scored Saturday night and Sun
day.


Rebels Attack in Waves.


The Wet Mini followed their
usual tactic of battering the
crumbling defenses with human
tidal waves.


The attackers hurled plastic
containers of nitroglycerine at
the barbed wire defenses as they
launched their drives.


The French fought back des-
perately. Wave after wave of
rebel attackers were raked by
murderous machinegun and ar
tillery fire, but still they came on.
The French met the rebels at
the barricadeS with savage bay
onet thrustS, as hand-to-hand
fighting ragged on all sides.


The attack was preceded last
night by the usual stepup in
rebel mortar and artillery fire on
the shrunken fortress defenses.


Both sides had rushed in re-
inforcements and supplies during
the lull in the fighting.


American-supplied transports
roared in to parachute more men
and tons of war materiel. The
new troops included nearly $50
men who had volunteered to aid
their battle-weary comrades.

RIO De JANEIRO, Brazil, Aug.
23.-Brazil's long-stewing polit-
ical crisis boiled over today with

Vargas and the army giving him
solid support.


For a time last night the guard
around the presidential palace
was doubled. but later the REIN
forcementS were withdrawn.
Early today only one civil guard

Army tanks were reported to

tons at the palace. but ap-
parently they turned back en-

Dental candidate and titular

Union (UDN). which is the chief
opposition to Gen. Vargas.
Assurances Broadcast.

tense capital, the government ra-

surances by Gen. Vargas mill

Castro, that all was calm at the
palace and pledges that the
armed forces would fulfill their
constitutional duty to uphold the
presidency.

army units to prepare to take

der lid of censorship and that

Military Leaders Confer.

sination plot against anti-Vargas

bubbling with bullish enthusiasm.

quiet and prices receded from

appeared in significant sections.

The market has been advance
ing steadily since mid-September
of last year, and that climb has
been accelerated in the past few
weeks.


A psychological factor was the
decrease yesterday by the Fed
eral Reserve in the charge it
makes for lending money to
commercial banks. which in turn
lend the money to business.

SAN DIEGO, Calf, Dec. 18.-
Undefeated Boiling Air Force
Base and Fort Sill, Okla, East
ern and Western military foot
ball champions. respectively, were
poised today for their battle here
tomorrow at Balboa Stadium in
the third annual Poinsettia Bowl
game.


Fort Sill, with its 11-0 record.

win the military championship
contest against the Airmen, who
have a seasons mark of 9-0-1.


"A crowd of 10000 is expected

ups are dotted with stars from

ond appearance in the Poin-
settia Bowl under Coach Roger
Antaya. In 1852 Boiling came

dog and walloped the San Diego
Naval Training Center, 35-14,
behind the brilliant passing of
AL Dorow. now of the Washing
ton Redskins.


O'Connell Leads Airmen.


This time, the Airmen have
brought along Tommy O'Connell,
recently awarded the most valu-
able player award in Air Force
football ranks. He is the former
All-America quarterback from
Illinois who later saw service
with the Chicago Bears. Boiling
Is placing most of the response
bility for a triumph on his trusty
throwing arm. O'Connell is not
unknown in these parts, having
played for Illinois In the 1862
Rose Bowl game against Stan
ford.


Arrayed against the offensive
minded Boiling team are such
nationally kpown ex-collegians
as Billy Vessels, Buck McPhail
and Leon (Mule Train) Heath,
all from Oklahoma. Vessels went
to Canada for a year of pro
football after his graduation,
McPhail spent season with the
Baltimore Colts and Heath
played fullback for the Washing
ton Redskins.


Originally, Fort Ord was looked
upon as the logical choice to
play Boiling in this game, but
Sill's overwhelming and unex-
pected success as the season pro-
gressed took Ord out of the run
ming. Ord actually lost the
chance to represent the West
when it was upset by the San
Diego Phib Pacs, 1921.

the Quantico Marines into camp
in its first game of the season,
Fort Sill started unspectacularly.
A big change came over the
Cannoneers in the third game
of the season when they wall
loped Sheppard AFB, $50. For
the first time Vessels flashed the
form that made him an out
standing collegiate.


After the Sheppard game Sill
got another boost when Marv
Matuszak, former All-America
guard at Tulsa and an outstand-
ing rookie with the Pittsburgh
Steelers, joined the squad. A
powerful defensive force was
nodded around Matuszak.


Sill's backf1eld Is rounded out
by Quarterbacks Dan Page, for
mer All-Southwestern star at
Texas, and Merrell Green from
Oklahoma. The latter is a con-
verted halfback.


After Sill got rolling eight of
its II opponents were completely
outclassed, including Fort Leon
ard Wood. Fort Bliss, Fort Car
son, Kessler AFB, Fort Hood,
twice, and the Brooke Army
Medical Center.


Tomorrow's game shapes up as
q duel between Vessels and
O'Connell, with the former
heading up q strong ground
game and the latter laying down
an air barrage.

October is the brilliant sunset OF the.

and winter-berTy. s


October Is full Of misty mornings
when the hills rise like islands from
the valley fog. The October moon
seems brighter and the stars are be-
ginning to glitter with the sparkle Of
December. The long complaint Of the
katydid dies away In October. and the
nights are left to the sighing winds.


Squirrels thrash through the tree.
tops on urgent autumn business. %
full Of life that they cry challenge to
each other from leafless treetops and
race along the whip-thin branches.
Chipmunks hurry their late harvest
and line their nests with silk-weed
nun and thistle down for cold nights
to come.


! October brings Indian Summer.
when the hills are blue and smoke
hangs like 9 haze and the air is mild
as May. It comes and goes and then
returns-th strange magic Of Oc-
tober weather: between those Indian
Summer interludes the frost lies sharp
and cleaning on the land. For October
is autumn at its peak, brilliant and
blue and nany-colored and crisp and
misty and full Of sweet-scented lowell
ness.

treaty last night when the grand

many.

duced in the Italian Chamber of

expected until the fall, after

There are genuinely significant implica-
lions, political and military, behind the joint
announcement that Turkey and Pakistan have
agreed to seek methods for achieving "closer
friendly collaboration"


OF the two, the military implications are
the more obvious ones but the political mean
ings of this developing alliance may prove more
far-reaching and may have greater impact upon
the course of world affairs While the Ankara-
Karachi communique itself made no mention
of the religious bond between the two nations,
there was pointed reference to it in the informal
comment which followed. Both countries are
overwhelmingly Moslem. They are also bluntly
anti-Communist and clearly pro-Western as
far as the cold war is concerned. Neither suffers
from paralyzing inhibitions of the spirit or from
a philosophy of doing nothing for fear OF
offending Moscow and Peiping.


References to the "Mosem world" and the
latent power which it possesses have cropped
up frequently in the years since World War II
ended There has, however, been no real CO.
hesion of the Moslem countries stretching
roughly from Northwest Africa to 1ndonesia.
Some are not even fully independent and few
have achieved real political maturity. The only
tangible effort to create union of these coun-
tries came with formation of the Arab League
in 1915. Rivalries within this group and

Der countries have prevented the league from
becoming the strong force it might have been
or even becoming the hard core of the "Moslem
world"


Turkey and Pakistan, Moslem but not
Arab, may become this very core" through
the workings of their new agreement. They
have let it be known that they would welcome
other partners of like political convictions into
their alliance. Iraq, member of the Arab
League, and Iran a non-Arabic Moslem coun-
try, already nave indicated interest. Saudi
Arabia, another member of the league and
Afghanistan, another Moslem country have
been mentioned If some or all of these nations
do attach themselves to the Turkey Pakistan
a unified "Moslem world" The political influ-
ence of such a grouping could become much
greater than their presently divided powers.


Meanwhile, from the military standpoint,
the Ankara- Karachi agreement promises tan
gible values to the free world. Turkey, already
member of NATO and in process Of undermining
her defense establishment, shares frontiers with
Communist nations both in Europe and Asia.
Pakistan whose Prime Minister has now an
nounced an official request for American mill
tary aid-despite midas bitter objections-is
Just behind the mountains from Asiatic Russia
and Red China. Iran, which is receiving
American equipment and training help, links
Turkey and Pakistan and likewise borders
Asiatic Russia. The formulating of an alliance
among these three, and perhaps others in the
area, could eventually produce q strong and
deep defense front.
headline: An Alliance to Watch

The tentative agreement between the
District Commissioners and the National
Capital Planning Commission over Potomac
River bridge sites has been given official
Senate sanction by unanimous vote. All
that remains now to give the pact statutory
permanency is the concurrence of the
House. Since that body already had ap-
proved the Jones Point bridge, one of the
two structures provided for in the Senate
bill, there is little doubt that the House
will extend its approval to include the
once controversial central-area bridge. All
will be quiet once more along the Oft
embattled shores of the Potomac.


There are still problems to be worked
out by District and NCPC officials respect
ing the central-area site. The understand
ing reached recently by the two feuding
sides was on principles only. That is, both
parties finally agreed that traffic between
Washington and Virginia requires imnle-
diate planning and construction of span
somewhere between the Memorial and Key
Bridges. Both sides also agreed that the
bridge would not be placed over or directly
adjacent to Theodore Roosevelt Island, the
Wildlife sanctuary which the Theodore
Roosevelt Memorial Association was pre-
pared to defend to its last breath. The
bridge therefore will have to be put some
where downstream from little South
Island, lower tip of the Theodore Roosevelt
Island group, yet far enough above the
Memorial Bridge as not to detract from
that structure. The new bridge will be tied
in with Twenty fourth street, which, under
the agreement, will become key link in
the inner traffic loop around downtown
Washington. At the Virginia end there
will be no major changes in the original
plans for connections with Arlington boule-
ward and the George Washington Memorial
parkway.


The bridge authorization will have to
be backed up later by appropriations, of
course, but no obstacles are foreseen in
that direction. Once the House joins in the
Senate action and the President adds his
signature to the legislation, definite plan
ming for the long-needed central and Alex
andria bridges can start That will be
happy day for bottlereck-weary motorists
who cross the, river every day.

reported near death today in

heart trouble and is nearly blind
with cataracts.


Won Neurath suffered a heart
attack in his cell last week.
Friends said he was being
treated with drug injections and
emergency oxygen but his con-
dition is critical.


His wife and daughter were
called from West Germany to
Berlin last Thursday. Since then
they have kept a death watch
outside Spandau.


Won Neurath, who was also
Hitler's protector" of occupied
Czech provinces, was sentenced
eight years ago at the Nuern-
berg war crimes trial to IS years
Imprisonment.

mosa. One broadcast said 9

MED that any ships were hit.

the Communists may try to con-
quer Quemoy. If they think they

The French poured reinforce
ments into the vital Red River
delta today as speculation grew
that massing Wet Mini legions
would strike there within the
next few weeks.


French Union sources pre-
dicted the Communicated rebels
would launch their expected big
thrust before the monsoon rains
hit their peak at the end OF
June. If they don't, they will
probably have to wait until the
monsoon season ends in early
October.


Several large rebel units which
helped destroy the French bas-
ton of Diem Bien Phu 220 miles
west of Hanoi are already back
at their old posts on the Thanh
Hoa plain. They form part of
an arc the Wet Mimi is weld
ing around the rice-rich delta.
/, French military sources said
the returning units were drawn
from various regiments to boil
ster the Wet Mimi assault on
Diem Bien Phu which finally
fell May 7.


Gen. Paul Ely, the new French
Union commander in chief, flew
to the Delta area yesterday to
inspect defense preparations in
three strategic zones. He is ex-
pected to return to Paris within
10 days to report on the delta
defenSeS.


Rebel units returning from
Diem Bien Phu were spotted sew
eral days ago at Sam Neua. 80
miles south of the fallen for
tress. There was speculation at
first that they might veer south
westward toward Laos and
lanuch another invasion of that
kingdom. Instead they kept
heading eastward to the Thanh
Hoa PLAIN south of the delta.


Other Wet Mimi troops from
Diem Bien Phu were reported
in the Hoa Binh area 35 miles
southwest of Hanoi. while some
were reported moving around
Pluto, As miles northwest of the
city.


French warplaneS were sent
out in force yesterday to pound
Route IL leading from Diem
Bien Phu to the delta.

Two new quakes shook the bat
tered north Algerian city of Or
leansville last night, injuring at
least two persons, crumpling
and knocking out communica-
tions.


The shocks were the strongest
since the disastrous upheaval
which hit Orleansville and sur
rounding villages last week, leav-
ing more than 1.400 dead and
5000 injured.


Buildings which had been
badly damaged in the first quake
collapsed last night. They in
cluded local government Offices
and Orleansville College.


The new tremors spread panic
among some 10000 homeless vic
tins of the last quake who have
been living in tents outside Or
leanSville.


Small shocks have been felt
every day since last weeks
quake. but this was the first to
do any damage.

controversy over German rearmament

NEW YORK, Nov. 25.-An
armed showdown by Communist
leaders in the Kremlin settled
the Moscow struggle for power
and sent Police Boss Lavrenty p.
Beria to his doom, says a former
officer of Beria's forces.


Writing in Life Magazine, 1t.
Col. Yuri Rastvorov, who detected
to the Americans In japan last
January. declares:


Beria, allied with Stalin's son.
1t. Gen. Vastly Stain, gathered
forces during Stalin's final ILL
ness with the intention even
tually of seizing the Soviet gov
ernment by force. Marshal
Georgi Zhukov and other mill
tary leaders, fearing a blood
purge even greater than Stalin's
If Beria succeeded, Joined forces
with Georgi Malenkov and other
Communist elements to thwart
the intended coup, seized Beria
and his cohorts and send them
to death by execution.


Believes Death Natural.


Col. Rastvorov until last jan
uary was the head of an MVD
(Beria's secret police) spy ring
In Japan. Expressing conviction
that Stain died a natural death
in March. 1858. he says:


With 10 physicians prepared
to testify that their leader had
indeed died Of a brain hemor-
rliage, each member Of the
(ruling) group hoped to fore
stall any future accusations
that he had plotted Stains
death or failed to provide the
fullest possible medical care for
the dying vozhd leader).


But a contest for power be-
tween the various blocs became
inevitable when Stain died. Col.
Rastvorov sketches the Kremlin
events this way:


Malenkov, who had flattered
and wooed Beria In the past,
had his assistance in becoming
premier, while Eeria retained
control over the secret police
and the nations arms program.
Beria realized the time was not
ripe for a hated police boss to
take over the top job, and thus
Joined a working agreement
with Malenkov and v. NJ. Molo-
tov for governing triulnvirate.


Molotov could not have taken
the top job because he had been
In disfavor and his wife ectu-
ally had just been released from
Imprisonment on Stalin's char
ges that she was a spy for the
Americans. This charge was
based largely on the fact that
she had brother in the United
States.


Got Doctors Acquitted.


But Beria set out at once to
build up his own power. quietly
shaking up police forces
throughout the country, and
climaxing his moves by bringing
about public acquittal of the
group of doctors accused III
February, 1858, of plotting So
Wet leaders deaths.


Aligned with Beria were
Stalin's son and several generals,
including Col. Gen. Pavel Arte-
miev, commandant of the Mos
COW district; 1t. Gen. N. K.
Spiridonov. commandant of the
Kremlin, and 1t. Gen. K. r.
Sinilov. commandant of the city
of Moscow. (None of these has
been heard from since Beria was
seized. Rastvorov reports all
were quietly liquidated.)


But Malenkov was not. idle
either, and set about strength
ening his position in the Com
munist Party. Suddenly, with
the help Of army general, Malen-
kov had young Stain removed
from his post. Beria realized the
time for action had come, and
Artemiev ordered two divisions
under trusted officers into Mos
COW from the nearby provinces.
But Communist spies In the
army tipped off Malenkov.


Zhukov, along with Defense
Minister Nikolai Bulganin and
other high army officers. secretly
brought in two loyal guards divi-
sions from the Urals region, one
o fthem a tank division. They
arranged to capture Beria by
calling a full meeting of the
party central committee. That
was June 26, 1858.


Key Communist leaders were
armed as they gathered for the
meeting. They seized Beria on
his arrival. With Beria gone, the
plot collapsed.

Phu had inflicted heavy losses"
on the Wet Mimi and smashed
a network of rebel trenches on
the eastern side of the dustbowl.


French infantrymen. spear
headed by tanks and after three
hours of artillery bombardment,
attacked the Communist : led
Wet Mimi and at the point of
bayorets drove them from hill
position in the east.


The Wet Mimi then were driven
out of a series of winding
trenches in bloody hand-to-hand
fighting.


French Losses "Appreciable."


The French high command
announced that the losses Of
the attacking French forces
were "appreciable."


Earlier the French announced
that the Red-led Wet Mimi
staged a sneak attack on the
main air strip at the fortress
last night and blew up the
northern section. They said the
rebels did this by placing bam-
boo poles stuffed with nitro
glycerine under the fields steel
mating. The damage less than
tWo-thirds of a mile from the
heart of the fortress was .e-
paired despite a Red artillery
barrage.


However, planes have been
unable to land at Diem Bien Phu
for some time because of the
heavy Wet Mini Smelling and
the French have had to supply
the fortress by parachute.


Despite the steady hammering
OF key French positions there
was no immediate indication
that fresh general assault was
imminent.


French Strike Back.


The French hit back yesterday
with their own heavy artillery
fire and relentless plane attacks
in an effort to upset the time
table of the Wet Minis Com
munist commanders.


Behind their battered ram
parts, French Union troops also
feverishly rushed work on their
own dugouts, underground bunk
ers and trenches. These have
been riddled by Wet Mimi shells
and were battered under the
furious infantry attacks which
ended abruptly six days ago.


The French yesterday sent out
strong reconnaissance units to
the west and elsewhere around
Diem Bien Phu. But the Wet
Mimi showed little interest in
these expeditions. holding their
fire and saving ammunition for
a general assault. The French
reported mo enemy contacts"


Supplies Dropped.


More ammunition and other
supplies were parachuted to the
fortress yesterday from French
transports and giant flying box
cars piloted by American civilian
airmen.


Observers said If the French
can hammer back one more mass
attack by the Wet Mimi, the
crisis should be over. Until
this next assault has been with
stood, however. the situation for
the defense, force is considered
highly dangerous"

MANILA, Sept. 3.-A heavily
loaded logging train carrying
more than 100 passengers on
empty fiat cars careened down a
mountainside and piled up on a
wooden bridge yesterday, killing
at least 80 persons.
Most Of the others were in
jured, many critically. in what is
described as the worst railroad
disaster in Philippines history.
Cars, logs and crushed bodies
hurtled from the wrecked bridge
into a gorge 100 feet below.
Cranes were hoisting massive
logs from the gorge today and
officials said additional bodies
may be uncovered.


The wreck occurred on north
ern Negros Island in the south
ern Philippines and authorities
still were trying to piece to-
gether exactly what happened.


Engineer Pablo Villarete. 46,
said that as his train crept down
steep grade near the town
of Fabrica 16 cars loaded with
logs broke loose and began roll
ing free. In an attempt to save
his train he said he raced his
engine and seven coupled cars
down the mountain, but the
runaway cars caught up with.
the train on the bridge. -


The crash derailed many cars,
wrecked the bridge and tossed
five cars over the side. Chains
holding the logs snapped and, the
huge logs hurtled off the cars,
crushing many passengers and
sweeping others into the gorge.
Some cars were smashed against
the mountainSide.


officials said passengers on the
train were mostly employees of the
Insular Lumber Co., which owned
the train, and their wives and
children.

AS the world faces the increasing
uncertainties of the atomic age, the
public mind is alternately gripped by
hope and despair. This was the case
last Week--as usual. And the week
ended without any great change
from the situation that had pre-
vailed seven days earlier There was


depending on how one looked at
it-Sound reason for either emotion,
hope or despair.

week. William F. Knowland, Repub-
lican Senate majority leader, in
terrupted the Mccarthy censure de-
bate with a.maverick warning that

ciliatory toward the Soviet Union.
Like-minded Republicans took up
the cry. 8,


But later there was swing to OPP
timism, In the United Nations, the
first significant steps toward shar-
ing the benefits Of atomic peace

264-4. in favor of the Paris agree
ments providing for 500,00O-man
West German army to- bolster the
anti-Communist North Atlantic
community.


But the most hopeful moments
came Friday, in Bonn and in WASH
lngton. In the former city, German

agreements. His coalition govern

three Of the four parties involved

affirmed Adenauer's strength. Two
OF the three rebel parties voted with

Free Democrats and one Of Herr
Adenauer's own Christian Demo-
Gratis, abstained.


And in Washington French Pre-
mier Pierre Mendes- France prom
ised that his National Assembly
would ratify the Paris agreements
before the end Of the year. He also
agreed informally to reject Russia's
plan for talks which would delay
ratification.


But these happy closing notes
could not dispel the memory of

A Navy Neptune bomber crashed
into the sea yesterday about 200
yards from shore and the crew
of 10 men perished.


Six bodies had been recovered
from the water last night and
others were sighted trapped in
the submerged wreckage. Diving
crews, flown here from Key
West, worked throughout the
night in an attempt to recover
the remaining bodies.


The two-engined plane ap-
parently crashed shortly after
taking off from Windsor Field,
headquarters for anti-submarine
exercises being conducted in the
Bahamas.


Immediately after the plane
was reported missing, a search
was ordered and an area of 800
miles radius was combed for it
but not until noon was the
wreckage spotted off Clifton
Pier on the southern coast of
the island.


Names of the victims will be
announced today from Wash
ington following notification of
next of kin.

After many years spent In dull,
undressing obscurity, bath
rooms are at last coming into
their own as a focus for decora-
tive attention.


Durable new materials have
been developed that offer high
fashion designs and colors max
ing possible a bathroom with new
good looks that relate closely to
the rest of the living area.


Most noteworthy trend today
Is toward built-in sinks, recessed
in wide counter tops over wall
to-Wau cabinets. These double
as convenient dressing tables and
offer streamlined storage for
linens, medicines and often laun-
dry hampers below.


Surfacing these new built-in
units, and on wall areas and
floors. are handsome sturdy plas-
tics. Formica plastic Is now
available in a new range of
bright high-style colors like
Siamese pink, charcoal, spruce,
citron and pumpkin. Also, in

marble and mosaic motifs that
are growing in fashion for living
room schemes. Vinyl tiles for the
floor, easy to install, provide vivid
color palette ranging from newly
popular pinks to rich heige-to-
brown wood colorings.

gaining attention. A new pint
sized version of the popular self
squeezing mop, with all the sturdy
construction of the conventional
size and a few. tricks of its own
added, has been specially de-
signed for bathroom use. With a
rubber hanging tip for storage
on a hook, or out of sight be-
hind the shower curtain, the
sponge mop is a handy tool for
scrubbing the tub, hopping walls,
and efficient cleaning of those
difficult bathroom floors. An
extension handle gives it flexible
reach.


Even without a major re-
modelling, current bathrooms can
be given a fresh viewpoint with
q few new decorative elements.
Cafe curtains on bright brass
rings, lowered wood shutters
and painted bamboo blinds COM
pete for window honors. Richly
colored washable cotton carpet
ing with nonslip rubber backing
is used for oversize rugs and
even wall-to-wall effects are
popular. Shower curtains reflect
new high-style fabric designs
like harlequin patterns and alb
stract motifs, and will be avail
able this year in woven chintz
and sailcloth, some trimmed in
ball fringe for a formal feeling.


Conversation piece accessories
are borrowed from every room in
the house and every period. Or

aimed at holding last weeks
gains, the ingot rate this week

of rated capacity.


The steel business is improving
gradually but this is scarcely
noticeable from week to week,

added. the market is definitely
stronger and the production
trend is up.


In best demand, the weekly
said, are galvanized sheets, oil
country goods, structural shapes
and tin mill products. Recent
signs of easing, however, have
been shown by all these products
except tinplate.

year but came back strong re-

tober /.

sheets, which had been quite
easy. are firming noticeably; hot
rolled sheets and strip are still
soft, as are most sizes and types
of bars; but sheets are expected

automotive industry.

The proposed "reappraiSap or COM

The Chest program in Washington and its
suburbs has been suffering from the same
sort of stresses and strains that public serv-
ices generally have felt with the rapid
growth Of the whole region. The fund
raising, budgeting and welfare planning OF
the federated Chests are based on policies

Actually, we are less consolidated here

the country Whereas other large cities and
their suburbs usually have one chest to
serve the whole urban and suburban region,
the divided political setup in Greater Wash
ington has led to the creation OF separate
chests for the Virginia, Maryland and Dis
trict portions of the Metropolitan Area.
The six local chests are tied together
loosely by the Chest Federation. which con-
ducts the campaigns and distributes the
money according to needs. Because each OF
the chests maintains its own headquarters
and performs certain administrative work,
the aggregate administrative costs here are
greater than in some other large cities.
This has led to suggestions that one overall
chest to serve the whole region would be
preferable to the present arrangement.
Countering the one-chest idea are proposals
that suburban communities conduct their
own campaigns. But such trend would be
out Of line with the developing theory In
public-service quarters that Washington and
its suburbs compose one great city, with
common objectives and common problems
that should be tackled on a regional team
work basis.


The planned study by committee
representing ali the chests will be helpful IN
considering recent campaign, budgeting and
planning difficulties. It should aid in clear
ing the air of rumors that eventual dissolu-
ton of the federation is possibility Ger
tainly any plan involving the holding OF six
separate chest campaigns would be unthink-
able. What is needed Is fewer campaigns,
not more of them.

something else Is bound TO

LONDON. Sept. 9.-Britain
has given up the idea Of
assembling a nlne-power confer
ence by next Tuesday on West
German rearmament.


The Bonn government raised
objections to such an early
meeting while Paris and Wash
ington showed no enthusiasm
for it.


Official sources said yesterday
that Prime Minister Churchill's
cabinet had decided at a three
hour meeting not to cancel per-
manently the proposed London
conference aimed at salvaging
the French-rejected plan for
bringing West German divisions
into a unified European army.


Britain had wanted quick talks
to hammer out an alternative
to the European Defense Com
munity plan, which the French
National Assembly killed, before
the United Nations General AS
sembly meets September 81.


Sir Winston and his minister
agreed that a final decision on
Germany's role in western de-
Tense must rest with the North
Atlantic Treaty Organization,
the informants said. But they
stuck to their view that a con-
ference in London confined to
the six countries which signed
the EDO treaty, plus the United
States, Britain and Canada. could
do useful preparatory work.


West German officials said
Chancellor Konrad Adenauer. had
asked the United States and
British high commissioners for
more time for extensive diplo-
matte exchanges with other in
terested nations before facing
the French again over a con-
ference table.


French foreign ministry off,
Gals said Premier Pierre Mendes-
France was ready to meet with
the other eight suggested for
eign ministers in London Tues
day. but felt little time remained
to prepare for the conference.

For Federal workers, the Korean

Many of them have been working
for Uncle Sam since 1850, when
Congress approved a law prohibits
ing permanent appointments The

dreds Of thousands of persons hired

permanent appointments. Presi-
dent Eisenhower last week ordered
