worked for the Government three
years or more and who have passed
their civil service exams be rated
career" employees. Those with more
than one and less than three years,
who were hired off civil service rolls,

and will automatically graduate to
career rank at the end of their third
year.


Any Government worker who does
not now rate career or career-indef-
mite status will have a chance to
qualify by taking civil service ex-
aminations and by serving out the
necessary time.


Some $4,000 persons in Washing

designations. Altogether, about 220,-

ents are gradually waking up to the

The Montgomery County public
school system has been described from

lively costly" or "a bargain" Actually,
the county's pitiful public education
system is not only Excessively costly"
in misspent tax dollars. but is also
almost criminally wasteful in misspent
time of American students.

sons, have been made painfully aware

instruction and the over abundance of

May I suggest that county taxpayers

emily wasted in Montgomery County

spent in county public schools?


Franklin T. Miles.

"A dynamite charge exploded on

ing a second when the explosion
came.

dent for Tennessee Gas, said the
crew apparently drilled into a
hole that already had dynamite
in it.


The charges usually are set off
by remote control after the boat
has moved to safe position.


A supply barge. loaded with
5000 pounds of dynamite. was
tied to the boat. It didn't ex-
plode. The boat was badly dam
aged, but stayed afloat.





Milton Swain, %. apparently
was the only survivor. He said
seven other men aboard ap-
parently were either drowned or
blown to bits. The boat usually
carried a crew of eight.


Knocked Into River.

into the river, was brought to a
hospital here where his condi-
ton was reported "fair."


Charlie Roberts, funeral home
operator here, said one badly
mangled body has been removed
from the drill rigging.


Rescue units began dragging
the river for other bodies after
an explosive expert checked the
dynamite barge.

The President and Mrs. Eisen-
hover entertained at the first
State reception of 1854 and 1t
will probably turn out to be the
most pleasant.


The party, known as the de-
partmental reception honors
many government departments
but in comparison, the guests
number few. The actual count
last evening was 963, whereas the
average is above 1900.


The Chief Executive and his
Lady descended the White House
staircase to the stirring blare Of
drums and bugles at the ap-
pointed hour of 9 o'clock. BY
this time all guests had assembled
in the East Room waiting to be
received.


Pause in Main Hall


The President and Mrs. Eli
senhower paused in the center of
the main hall as the red
coated Marine band struck up
Hail to the Chief" and then
marched into the Blue Room to
receive their guests.


First to come down the stairs,
which is, unfortunately, almost
hidden from view, were four
service men, one from each
branch, with the Presidents
flag and the Stars and Stripes.
They were followed by the Eli
SenhowerS, then members of the
cabinet and finally the White
House aides.


This reception was for officials
of the Treasury, Post Office, In
terror, Agriculture, Commerce,
Labor, and Welfare Departments
and certain other Federal agen-
cies. All the cabinet members
and their wives of these depart
ments were there with the ex-
ceptions of the BensonS of
Agriculture and the Mitchells of
Labor. Others of the presiden-
tial family present were the
Secretary of Defense and Mrs.
Wilson and the Attorney General
and Mrs. Brownell.


AS the members of the cabinet
arrived by the front entrance,
they were ushered upstairs to
the Presidents library, first leav-
ing their coats to be hung on a
coat rack which could be viewed
by all. Even the recent renova-
ton of the White House did not
correct this eye sore in the
presence of all the pomp and
glory which surrounds state
functions.


White Tie ond Tolls


The dress for the evening was.
of course, white tie and tails for
the men. and the ladies were in
their most gala evening gowns.


Mrs. Eisenhower, on the arm
of her husband, looked particu-
larlly pretty in a coral under
black lace evening gown. She
wore black net gloves which
reached above her elbows, but
she removed them before shaking
hands with the guests.


Members of the cabinet went
through the line first and then
continued through the Red Room
and finally into the State Din
ing Room. Here they met and
mingled with friends from their
Offices and others. This informal
chatting is unfamiliar at a White
House event and probably was
one reason why the party was SO
pleasant and why the top officials
stayed on at the reception.


The President and Mrs. Eli
senhower received this group and
with more than just a how-do-
you-do to many, in an hour and
five minutes. They took three
breaks to timber their hands and
catch their breaths.


Firm Hand Token


At few minutes after 10 sew
eral aides very politely but firmly
formed an aisle across the hall
between the entrance to the
Red Room and doorway on the
other side which leads to an
elevator.


AS though a button had been
pushed, the door opened and the
President and his wife walked
forward and returned to their
living quarters via the elevator

SENO, Indo- China. Jan. 19.-
French union forces attacking
with tanks drove today within
6 miles of Thakhek. on the
Thailand- -Indo- China border 40
miles north of Seno. The French
are making a sweep aimed at re-
covering control of Central Laos
territory lost to the Wet Mimi.


Gen. Andre Franchi, the
French commander, launched the
drive on Saturday. Thus far his
troops have encountered little
resistance. He said the Commu-
nist-led Wet Mimi may not try
to defend Thakhek. But I'm
taking nothing for granted be-
cause the Wet Mimi may charge
like a wounded boar"


The Wet Mimi drove the
French from Thakhek and the
surrounding area in a surprise
drive just before Christmas that
split Indo-China in two. The
French did not defend Thakhek.
but now Franchi'S aim is to
regain the lost territory.


Earlier reports said the Wet
M.nh did not remain in Thakhek
but they might try to keep the
French out of the devastated
town. which commands the Me-
kong River.


Other French union forces fam
nng out to the north had crossed
the Senoi River 80 miles north
east of Seno, the French held
Laotian fortress.


In Hanoi, a French Army
spokesman said the heavy
bombings and Strafing of the
Wet Mimi around Diem Bien Phu
had upset the rebels timetable
for an assault on that last big
French stronghold in North
western Indo-C China.

The Supreme Courts SiX-to-tWo decision In
the Laburnum Construction Corporation case
constitutes a sharp warning to irresponsible
labor organizers that Federal labor relations
laws will not protect them from damage suits
for wrongful tactics. It is hard to understand
why there could have been any dissenting opin-
ions on this fragrant example. of violent union
ism in Breathitt County, Kentucky. Even the
dissenters conceded that the union had used
unfair labor practices, specifically threats and
the force of picket line to make employees join
a union contrary to their desires" But that
was not all. The threats and actions put the
Laburnum firm out of business in the Kentucky
mine fields The majority Of the court rightly
held that the offending union could-and
should-be held accountable for damages done
the firm.


Justice Burton, on behalf of the majority
with Justice Jackson taking no part in the de-
cision) upheld the Virginia Supreme Court OF
Appeals in affirming an award of $129,326 COM
pensatory and punitive damages to the La
burnum concern, Virginia corporation The
United Construction Workers, an affiliate OF the
United Mine Workers, appealed the monetary
award on the ground that the Labor Manage
ment Relations Act of 1947 gave the National
Labor Relations Board exclusive jurisdiction In
all such labor disputes, even to the extent OF
precluding tort litigation in State courts. The
majority ruled to the contrary.


In the light Of the shocking events detailed
In the majority opinion, the unions claim to
immunity from damage liability was presump-
tuous to say the least. The facts as established
by the evidence, were that the Laburnum hrm
after being awarded a 100000 mine construc-
ton project and being promised second job
involving 100000 in Breathitt County, entered
into an agreement with American Federation OF
Labor unions for hiring workers: that when the
first contract was nearly completed in July of
1949 the UNIV affiliate suddenly announced its
intention Of CLOSING down" the project unless
the ALL was thrown out and the UNIV union
given control that the threats were carried out
by ga very rough, boisterous crowd" some MEM
bers Of which used abusive language, were drunk
and carried guns and knives: that as result OF
the demonstrations the mining companies,
themselves threatened with being closed down,
reluctantly Cancelled further contracts with the
Laburnum outfit.


Despite this factual background the mi
nority commended that Congress intended only
to give the NLRB what in this case would have
been ineffective authority to act. Granting
apprieved parties the right to sue the dissenting
opinion said, would only keep old wounds
open." But the majority effectively settled the
question Of congressional intent by quoting
statements Of the late Senator Taft and other
advocates of the legislation that clearly showed
that the Federal law was designed to supple
ment, not supplank State laws. including those
providing for civil damage suits.

This Capital City of the United States
lost one Of it's great personalities when
Helen Nicolay died at 88. Though she was
born in Paris, Washington was her home
through all but her infant years. Here she
served her father, Abraham Lincoln's Sec
retary, as faithful literary aide. At the
Art Students League here she learned to
draw and to paint. In the First Presby


terian and All Souls Unitarian Churches
here she developed her natural skill for
religious and ethical teaching. For local
children she reverently reWrote the Bible
and produced interpretive biographies of
national heroes which eventually had
readers around the world. Here she found
expression for her enthusiasm for music
and the drama. In the Washington Lit
erary Society she improved her powers Of
constructive criticism. Here she discovered
the joys of friendship with Florence Spof-
ford, Elisabeth Winship Tibbott, Frances
Downes, Julia Green, Fay Pearce Beij and
her devoted household retainers, Sophie
and Janey. Her famous partieS-unforget-
table occasions of wit and merriment-were
given here at the Woodward and the Ken
nedy- Warren. She was legendary figure
in Washington through eight colorful dec
AIDES, giving of herself with unlimited gen.
eroSity and receiving in return the tribute
of general popularity and affection.


basic principle Of American civiliza-
ton appears to have been demonstrated in
Miss Nicolay from first to last. She lived
and worked within tradition Of service.
In small things as well as in big things,
she contributed to the welfare and progress
of the entire national community. Modest,
provoked and offended by praise she was
tireless in deserving of responsive good will.
A few hours before she died she was talking
with her secretarial companion about re-
commencing new book to be entitled "The
Children That Lincoln Knew" In that
regard as in many, many others, she was
a link in chain reaching from the remot-
est past into the most distant conceivable
future and thus perhaps unwittingly q
bright example for her contemporaries,

Announcement that the National
Security Council is putting finishing

plan was greeted with mixture of
approval and evaporation by almost
all persons concerned.
I. Approval, because every one
thought it was on the whole good
plan: evaporation, because virtually
the same Reserve program is already
the law Of the land. a law that has
never been used.


The plan was worked up by the

Hannah, and by the Office Of De-
Tense Mobilization, the group which

In general, the plan has the backing

sion. The Presidents Endorsement

With all that approval the plan
must be a wonderful one. But. one
may we'll ask, If it's so ALTERED good,
why hasn't its already enacted twin
been put into operation and the
dangerous Reserve mess been
cleaned up?


The Reserve Story


Well. it's long story. And it
goes something like this:


Before World War II the military
Reserve wasn't much In size or quail
ity, but then neither was the regular
Army and Navy and the Nation did
not expect to use either. Then came
the frantic military buildup for the
war against the axis. Both the
Regulars and Reserves proved in
adequate, but there was enough time
to draft and train millions Of civil
ians who fought most Of the war. &.


After the peace Uncle Sam was
more Reserve conscious. The young
veterans were signed up for the Re
serves while they went through the
discharge procedure. All sorts of
grandiose plans for organizing and
training reserviSts were announced,
but none got to first base. The Re-
serves remained little more than q
long list of names, wrong addresses
and obsolete personal histories. And
twice Congress rejected q universal
military training bill.


Then. in 1850. Korea.


Again the Regulars were too small
in numbers. And this time there
was no chance to wait for the draft
ing and training of young civilians.
The reservists had to be thrown into
the breach.


Almost million reservists were
called, about 70 per cent Of them
veterans. The veterans were fathers,
essential workers. students, or just
plain men who had done their duty
once. But they fought while younger
men, who had never served, were
draft-deferred for being fathers, es-
sential workers and students.
Unfoirness Noted


Congress was deeply disturbed
by the unfairness Of 1t, and the law
makers in 1851 wrote a new law to
provide for universal military train
ing and service and In 1852 approved
a law recognizing the Reserve pro-
gram.


The UNITS law provided for six
months basic training Of all physi-
cally fit young men not needed for

The Commission on Judicial and Congress

concentration for higher pay for judges and
legislators was based mainly on considerations
as to what will best serve the national welfare.
The report stressed the benefits which would
accrue to the cause of better government, rather
than the benefits due underpaid public servants
on the bench and in Congress.


Voluminous testimony before the commits
sion showed the relationship between good gov
eminent and fair pay. Taking note OF testimony

ernmental salaries and those Tor comparable
private services and the resultant tendency OF
competent citizens to avoid public office, the
commission warned that the Government is the
loser by past shortsightedness. On this point
the commission said: zone of the most striking
and disturbing facts which the commissions
inquiry disclosed was the number of experienced,
able Federal judges and Congressman who have
been forced to abandon the public service solely
as a result of economic pressureS No one can
say how many more qualified candidates for
public office have been forced by these same
limitations to abandon any thought of Federal
service, though the evidence shows there have
been many" The group added that if the pres
ent trend of persons with judicial or legislative
ability to shun Federal service continues, the
result will be to further demorallze and weaken
essential areas of national leadership at time
when national responsibilities were never more
grave"


While the increases recommended were sub
stantial in every case, it was pointed out that
judicial and congressional pay raises have
Jagged far behind those for other Offices in and
out of Government. There have been five raises
for Government employees in general since the
last increase for judges and Congressman. The
policy has been in the past to adjust judicial
and legislative pay scales about once every 20
years. Meanwhile, rising living costs have been
no respecterS of persons.


Congress, always shy about voting itself
pay raise, will be glad to have the support Of
such an unbiased group as that headed by
Bernard G. Segal recently chancellor Of the
Philadelphia Bar Association and the II other

and the Kawasaki bomber
factory signed a contract today
that will launch Japan into jet
plane manufacture.


The. deal calls for Kawasaki to
make American F94 Starfire all
weather jet fighters and the fast
1913 jet trainer-the latter a ver-
sion of the F-80 Shooting Star.


"This program is greater than
any similar one so far negotiated
and when in operation it will
place Kawasaki in the forefront
of the great aircraft manu-
facturerS in the world" Lock-
heed representative said.


Under the contract, Kawasaki
gets all the rights to make the
two planes. as well as all the
technical help needed from Lock-
heed. Lockheed will also advise
on jet repair work now being
done for American warplanes at
Kawasaki's plant at Gifu, near
Nagoya.


Japan's once-great aircraft
companies were BACKED out for
eight years after World War II
ended, although few of them
have recently started sub-con-
tracing for United States Air
Force repair work.


This new agreement will give
Japan her first modern jet
factory.

To Make JET Planes

School officials are hoping the

grade school assistant principals

there aren't enough clerks now

Provide for Specialists.


WED like to see elementary

ings.


. Outlived Usefulness.

controversies from the public"

possibly giving a wrong impress

quainted with county govern

able to secure information from
the County Manager.

pro Of the leading pro-amateur

fields will reverse courses for

SYDNEY. Jan. 25.-Vic Seixas
and Tony Trabert advanced to

championships today. but the
new team of Bill Talbert of New
York and Australians Ken Rose
wall was trounced by the vet
eran Aussie pair Of John Brom-
wich and Adrian QuiSt.


SeiXaS and Trabert, Americas
unsuccessful Davis Cup team,
easily whipped Billy Knight and
Tony Pickard, English young
sters, 60, 6I3. Ga. The Eng
lish boys had no chance against
the American combination and
rarely were they able to get
even to deuce when Trabert or
Seixas was serving.


But Talbert and Rosewall
were. no match for Bromwich
and. Quist. who showed their
pre-World War II form with a
60. 6I3, 6-3 victory.

present. turned back Bob Perry

Fuel oil thrown on still-smoul.

five children to death and sent
their mothers and three other
children to the hospital with
serious burns.


Two other children fled from
the house and escaped injury.
Three of the dead were babies
less than a year old.


Mrs. G. B. Elmore. mother Of
three fire victims. was reported
in critical condition at a Dotham
(Ala.) hospital along with her
10-year-old daughter. Johnny
Lee.

Mrs. Roy Gilbert Of Eufaula,
who was an overnight guest in
the Elmore home with her
family. was badly burned and
two other children, Marcus. 2.
and Martha Helen, 2 months.
died in the flames.


The other Elmore children
burned seriously were Eugene
Allen, Z. and Alice Faye, about 5.


The other Elmore children
losing their lives in the fire were
listed as Ieannette and Annette.
9-month-old twins, and Doris. 3.
Those who escaped were Patri-
cha Elmore, 8. and May Isabel
Gilbert, 4.


2 Fathers Had Left.


The two fathers had left
earlier to go to a cafe for coffee.


Police Chief D. E. Nolen said
Mrs. Elmore used kerosene on a
fire which her husband had
made earlier. When the liquid
exploded che said her clothing
caught fire and she dropped the
can, spreading the oil and
flames.

HANOI, Indo- China. Mar. 10.
The Wet Mimi and the French
kept up their violent artillery
duel, at Diem Bien Phu today,
but there still was no resump-
ton Of massed rebel infantry
charges trying to overwhelm the
French Unions northwest Indo-
China fortress.


Under a full moon and q star
studded sky and on into the
morning the Smelling and heavy
French air strikes on the rebel
positions kept up around the
clock.


Some ground contacts yester-
day were reported. but they were
only clashes between advanced
French forces and small rebel
units on the south and south
west fringes of the French-held
plain. Some of these came with
in $50 yards Of French command
posts.


New Attack Anticipated.


The defenders still anticipated
another major Wet Mini effort
on the northern entrance to the
heart Of the fortress. The Wet
Mini hold hill positions in the
northern perimeter they cap
tured from the French early this
week in the battle which began
last Saturday.


Some French sources specu-
lated yesterday that the contin-
uing artillery barrage might be
covering a Wet Mini with
drawal. that Wet Mimi Gen. Vo
Nguyen Clap might have had
enough after losing an estimated
$4,000 dead or wounded-one-
fourth of the force he is believed
to have in the area.


But q French army spokesman
said last night the Wet Mini
still were rushing supplies by
coolie train and truck up to the
area, indicating. another mass
assault was in the offing. The
rebels broke off the desperate
do-or-die charges Wednesday
night.


Planes Hammer Foe.
> AS the artillery duel ragged,
French fighters and bombers
utilized the brilliant moonlight
and later bright sunlight, to
strafe, rocket and fire-bomb the
bulk of the rebel forces concen-
trated just north and northeast
Of the 6-by-4 mile oval plain.


Throughout the day the
French parachuted fresh troops,
ammunition and war supplies to
the besieged defenders. They
were still confident they could
continue to NOW down any fur
ther mass assaults and wreck
what has become the biggest Wet
Mini effort of the stalemated,
frustrating seven-year Indo-
China war.


Meanwhile. in the Red River
Delta, ITS miles to the east, the
French reported rebel sabotage
attacks ON 4he Hanoi-to-Hai-
phong highway. but said they
were being beat off. The French
said there was no interruption
to the flow of vital American
supplies.
